title: Super to be treated as a national asset
body:
O.P.
this post was edited
Apparently Mr Albanese thinks super should be treated as a "national asset".
At the annual superannuation lending roundtable this week, Mr Albanese urged the sector to invest more money in local corporate debt markets, arguing that there was “real potential to see these funds as a national asset that can be used more appropriately and get better returns as well, not just for individuals and for retirees, but for the nation”.
https://www.news.com.au/fina nce/economy/australian-econo my/dont-touch-albo-told-to-k eep-hands-off-super-after-he -urged-45-trillion-pool-to-b ecome-a-national-asset/news- story/1168184cdaa3700d6fd6c5d4470a4e48
It's just a remark and not yet policy. However, I note that the UK government has/will pass a bill that will allow the government, if necessary, to mandate some percentage of pension funds be invested in the UK. If it can happen there, it can happen here.
Instead, the Pension Schemes Bill will include a reserve power which would, if necessary, enable the government to set quantitative baseline targets for pension schemes to invest in a broader range of private assets, including in the UK, for the benefit of savers and for the economy.
https://www.gov.uk/governmen t/publications/pensions-inve stment-review-final-report/p ensions-investment-review-fi nal-report#investment-from-defined-contribution-schemes
I personally have mixed feelings about this.
On the negative side, it seems to undermine property rights. Surely people should have the right to choose where and how they invest for their retirement. Otherwise, why even have a super industry with different providers, funds, etc? Just nationalise the whole of super. Or better yet, take the lot of it as tax and use it to fund an age pension that actually keeps up with inflation.
My understanding is that (for now) super is our property and not for the government to control or interfere with. If it becomes acceptable for the government to suddenly dictate how super is invested, well what stops them from doing the same with all our investments? (I suppose that's a kind of "slippery slope" argument though.)
On the positive side, I suppose there's a decent chance that Australian equities and credit will perform well in future. We're a developed country with resources and infrastructure and our public market stock returns have been pretty good in recent history compared to the US and certainly compared to the world. Also I suppose there might hopefully be some positive externalities that benefit everyone here, such as jobs growth, infrastructure investment, innovation and attracting talented individuals from overseas.
What do you think of Mr. Albanese's ideas? If this looks to be going ahead, will it change how you allocate your assets in and out of super? Any general thoughts?
